think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: An 8-year-old boy in Nagaland, India presents with a 1-month history of cough, fever, headache, and right upper extremity paralysis (monoparesis), alongside a dietary exposure of consuming freshwater mountain crabs. In a high-incidence tuberculosis region, the combination of subacute fever, pulmonary symptoms, and a solitary isodense parietal mass lesion with surrounding vasogenic edema on brain CT led to a misdiagnosis of tubercular meningitis and cerebral tuberculoma, prompting empirical Category-II antitubercular therapy. The patient failed to improve, the BCG test was negative, and routine CBC revealed marked peripheral eosinophilia (17%) with elevated ESR (60 mm/hr). The critical challenge is differentiating an intracranial tuberculoma from cerebral and pulmonary trematodiasis caused by ectopic lung fluke migration.

2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint occurs upon completion of specialist triage evaluation at the referral hospital, including baseline hematology (showing 17% eosinophilia), ESR, negative BCG skin test, and brain CT showing the left parietal isodense lesion with edema, strictly prior to sputum microscopy for acid-fast bacilli and parasite ova, serum ELISA/immunodiffusion, and praziquantel administration.

3. Differential Distinctions:
- Central Nervous System Tuberculosis (Tuberculoma / Tubercular Meningitis): Primary initial presumption given chronic cough, fever, headache, and cerebral mass effect; ruled out by complete non-response to antitubercular therapy, negative BCG test, negative sputum AFB smears, and identification of trematode eggs in sputum.
- Pyogenic Brain Abscess or Intracranial Neoplasm: Considered for an isodense cerebral lesion with surrounding edema and focal motor deficit; excluded by significant peripheral eosinophilia (17%), dietary history of freshwater crab ingestion, and absence of marked neutrophilic leukocytosis.
- Neurocysticercosis: Common endemic parasitic cause of cerebral lesions; distinguished by dietary history (freshwater mountain crabs vs. porcine/fecal exposure) and confirmatory sputum trematode microscopy.
case_prompt:
An 8-year-old boy residing in Tuensang district, Nagaland, India, is brought for medical evaluation due to persistent cough, fever, headache, and sudden inability to move his right arm over the past month. His dietary history is notable for the consumption of freshwater mountainous crabs.

On physical examination, he is febrile and ill-appearing. Neurological examination demonstrates focal motor weakness of the right upper extremity (monoparesis) with preserved sensation.

Baseline hematological testing reveals a hemoglobin of 11 g/dL, a total leukocyte count of 8,800/mm³ with 58% neutrophils, 25% lymphocytes, and a marked peripheral eosinophilia of 17%. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is elevated at 60 mm/hr. A BCG skin test is non-reactive. A non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain reveals an isodense mass lesion with surrounding vasogenic edema in the left parietal lobe.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Central Nervous System Tuberculosis (Tubercular Meningitis / Tuberculoma)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered as the leading provisional diagnosis due to endemicity, fever, cough, and a mass lesion with edema on neuroimaging. Excluded by complete lack of response to antitubercular therapy, a negative BCG test, sputum smears negative for acid-fast bacilli, and microscopic discovery of trematode ova.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The patient was provisionally diagnosed as a case of tubercular meningitis. Without any laboratory investigations, he was discharged on 22 October, 2007 to be admitted in a Civil Hospital, Tuensang, on 25 October, where he was given antitubercular therapy (Cat-II). In the absence of any appreciable improvement, the patient was transferred on 6 November, 2007 to the Naga Hospital Authority

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Pyogenic Brain Abscess or Primary Intracranial Neoplasm
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered given the solitary isodense parietal lesion with mass effect and focal motor deficit. Excluded by the prominent peripheral eosinophilia of 17%, concurrent chronic pulmonary symptoms, dietary history of raw/undercooked crab consumption, and lack of polymorphonuclear leukocytosis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The routine hematological test revealed Hb 11gm%, total leucoctye count 8800 per cumm, neutrophils-58%, lymphocytes-25%, eosinophil-17%, and ESR (Westergren) 60 mm, at the end of the first hour. The BCG test was negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnostic turning point was the microscopic examination of sputum showing operculated Paragonimus eggs along with positive serum micro-ELISA and double immunodiffusion against Paragonimus heterotremus antigen in the setting of mountain crab ingestion, leading to complete clinical recovery following praziquantel therapy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Sputum samples were negative for AFB, but positive for Paragonimus eggs [Figure 2]. Micro-ELISA and double immunodiffusion tests of the serum were positive for paragonimiasis. Paragonimus heterotremus adult extract was used for these tests, as an antigen. The patient gave a history of consumption of mountainous crabs. Based on these findings, the case was finally diagnosed as pulmonary paragonimiasis with cerebral involvement.

editor_comments: Strict adherence to admission breakpoint. Presentation captures chronic cough, focal paralysis, eosinophilia, and brain CT findings prior to parasite microscopy. Direct verbatim quotes substantiate differentials and pivot.
